newsitem.title: USA: New York/Jersey job growth 0.9 pct in '97-NY Fed.
newsitem.headline: New York/Jersey job growth 0.9 pct in '97-NY Fed.

text.p: In part due to fewer government sector layoffs and company restructuring, New York and New Jersey states are likely to record a 0.9-percent job growth in 1997, according to an analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

"Although the nation's economy is projected to slow in 1997, the pace of employment in the New York-New Jersey region will remain stable," the research paper by New York Fed economists James Orr and Rae Rosen said.
"The job growth rate for the region will edge up to 0.9 percent in 1997," the Fed economists predicted.
Orr and Rosen estimated that job growth rose by a modest 0.8 percent in 1996.
"Although by no mean outstanding, this figure is impressive given the sizable losses in state and local government employment in the region in recent years," the economists pointed out.
According to the research paper, 21,000 government jobs were lost in New York/New Jersey in 1996 -- or about 40 percent of the public sector's 56,000 jobs that have disappeared since 1993.
"Government job losses should not offset employment gains in services and other sectors to the same extent as in 1996," the economists predicted.

"Within private industry, the outlook is mixed. manufacturing jobs will continue to disappear, though at a somewhat slower rate," they added, while expecting the pace of job creation in the service sector "although still the engine of job gains... will soften in 1997."
Orr and Rosen also said "the region's construction sector, however, is expected to expand at a moderate pace."
The New York Fed regional study also found:
-- the gap between the region's job growth and the nation's narrowed to 1.2 percent in 1996 from 1.7 percent in 1995 and should narrow further next year.
-- federal government job losses should total only 2,000 in 1997, down from 13,000 in 1996 and 23,000 the prior year.
-- state government job losses should amount to 5,000 in 1997 versus 11,000 in 1996.
-- manufacturing employment in the region will contract at about the same similar as in 1996 when 23,000 jobs were lost.
-- layoffs at transportation, public utilities and communications corporations are partly offset by job creation by small companies.
-- private education will outperform other segments of the service industry in terms of job creation.
-- new technology, financial deregulation, bank mergers and restructuring in the insurance industry will squeeze job creation in the financial service sector.
